# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

13 U.S. Code § 9 - Information as confidential; exception

  • U.S. Code
  • Notes
prev | next
(a) Neither the Secretary, nor any other officer or employee of the Department of Commerce or bureau or agency thereof, or local government census liaison, may, except as provided in section 8 or 16 or chapter 10 of this title or section 210 of the Departments of Commerce, Justice, and State, the Judiciary, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 1998 or section 2(f) of the Census of Agriculture Act of 1997—
(1)
use the information furnished under the provisions of this title for any purpose other than the statistical purposes for which it is supplied; or
(2)
make any publication whereby the data furnished by any particular establishment or individual under this title can be identified; or
(3)
permit anyone other than the sworn officers and employees of the Department or bureau or agency thereof to examine the individual reports.
No department, bureau, agency, officer, or employee of the Government, except the Secretary in carrying out the purposes of this title, shall require, for any reason, copies of census reports which have been retained by any such establishment or individual. Copies of census reports which have been so retained shall be immune from legal process, and shall not, without the consent of the individual or establishment concerned, be admitted as evidence or used for any purpose in any action, suit, or other judicial or administrative proceeding.
(b)
The provisions of subsection (a) of this section relating to the confidential treatment of data for particular individuals and establishments, shall not apply to the censuses of governments provided for by subchapter III of chapter 5 of this title, nor to interim current data provided for by subchapter IV of chapter 5 of this title as to the subjects covered by censuses of governments, with respect to any information obtained therefor that is compiled from, or customarily provided in, public rec­ords.
(Aug. 31, 1954, ch. 1158, 68 Stat. 1013; Pub. L. 87–813, Oct. 15, 1962, 76 Stat. 922; Pub. L. 101–533, § 5(b)(2), Nov. 7, 1990, 104 Stat. 2348; Pub. L. 103–430, § 2(b), Oct. 31, 1994, 108 Stat. 4394; Pub. L. 105–113, § 4(a)(1), Nov. 21, 1997, 111 Stat. 2276; Pub. L. 105–119, title II, § 210(k), Nov. 26, 1997, 111 Stat. 2487.)
Historical and Revision Notes

Based on title 13, U.S.C., 1952 ed., §§ 73, 83, 122, 208, 211, 252, and section 1442 of title 42, U.S.C., 1952 ed., The Public Health and Welfare (Aug. 7, 1916, ch. 274, § 3, 39 Stat. 437; Apr. 2, 1924, ch. 80, § 3, 43 Stat. 31; June 18, 1929, ch. 28, §§ 8, 11, 21, 46 Stat. 23, 25, 26; July 25, 1947, ch. 331, 61 Stat. 457; June 19, 1948, ch. 502, § 2, 62 Stat. 479; July 15, 1949, ch. 338, title VI, § 607, 63 Stat. 441; Sept. 7, 1950, ch. 910, § 2, 64 Stat. 784).

Section consolidates parts of sections 73 and 83 of title 13, U.S.C., 1952 ed., part of section 208 of such title, section 211 of such title, that part of section 122 of such title which made such sections 208 and 211 applicable to the quinquennial censuses of manufacturers, the mineral industries, and other businesses (see subchapter I of chapter 5 of this revised title), that part of section 252 of such title which made such sections 208 and 211 applicable to the quinquennial censuses of governments (see subchapter III of chapter 5 of this revised title), the second proviso in such section 252, and that part of subsection (b) of section 1442 of title 42, U.S.C., 1952 ed., which made such sections 208 and 211 applicable to the decennial censuses of housing (see subchapter II of chapter 5 of this revised title).

Words “except as provided in section 8 of this title” were inserted in opening phrase of subsection (a) for the purpose of clarity.

References to the Secretary, the Department of Commerce and bureaus and agencies thereof, and to other officers and employees of such Department, bureaus or agencies, were substituted for references to the Director of the Census, the “Census Office”, and the enumeration (in section 208 of title 13, U.S.C., 1952 ed.) of certain types of employees, for the purpose of completeness, and to conform with 1950 Reorganization Plan No. 5, §§ 1, 2, eff. May 24, 1950, 15 F.R. 3174, 64 Stat. 1263. See Revision Note to section 4 of this title.

The penal provisions of sections 73, 83, and 208 of title 13, U.S.C., 1952 ed., prescribing penalties for wrongful disclosure of information, are set out in section 214 of this title.

Changes were made in phraseology.

For remainder of sections 122, 208, and 252 of title 13, U.S.C., 1952 ed., and of section 1442 of title 42, U.S.C., 1952 ed. (which section has been transferred in its entirety to this revised title), see Distribution Table.

Editorial Notes
References in Text

Section 210 of the Departments of Commerce, Justice, and State, the Judiciary, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 1998, referred to in subsec. (a), is section 210 of Pub. L. 105–119, title II, Nov. 26, 1997, 111 Stat. 2483, which amended this section and enacted provisions set out as a note under section 141 of this title.

Section 2(f) of the Census of Agriculture Act of 1997, referred to in subsec. (a), is classified to section 2204g(f) of Title 7, Agriculture.

Amendments

1997—Subsec. (a). Pub. L. 105–119, which directed the substitution, in introductory provisions, of “of this title or section 210 of the Departments of Commerce, Justice, and State, the Judiciary, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 1998—” for “of this title—”, was executed by substituting “of this title or section 210 of the Departments of Commerce, Justice, and State, the Judiciary, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 1998” for “of this title” to reflect the probable intent of Congress and the amendment by Pub. L. 105–113. See below.

Pub. L. 105–113 inserted “or section 2(f) of the Census of Agriculture Act of 1997” after “chapter 10 of this title”.

1994—Subsec. (a). Pub. L. 103–430 inserted “or local government census liaison,” after “thereof,” and “or 16” after “section 8”.

1990—Subsec. (a). Pub. L. 101–533 inserted “or chapter 10” after “section 8”.

1962—Subsec. (a). Pub. L. 87–813 inserted sentences stating that no department, bureau, agency, officer, or employee of the Government, except the Secretary in carrying out the purposes of this title, shall require, for any reason, copies of census reports which have been retained by any such establishment or individual, and providing that copies of census reports which have been so retained shall be immune from legal process, and shall not, without the consent of the individual or establishment, be admitted as evidence or used for any purpose in any action, suit or other judicial or administrative proceeding.

13 U.S. Code § 224 - Failure to answer questions affecting companies, businesses, religious bodies, and other organizations; false answers

  • U.S. Code
  • Notes
prev | next

Whoever, being the owner, official, agent, person in charge, or assistant to the person in charge, of any company, business, institution, establishment, religious body, or organization of any nature whatsoever, neglects or refuses, when requested by the Secretary or other authorized officer or employee of the Department of Commerce or bureau or agency thereof, to answer completely and correctly to the best of his knowledge all questions relating to his company, business, institution, establishment, religious body, or other organization, or to records or statistics in his official custody, contained on any census or other schedule or questionnaire prepared and submitted to him under the authority of this title, shall be fined not more than $500; and if he willfully gives a false answer to any such question, he shall be fined not more than $10,000.

(Aug. 31, 1954, ch. 1158, 68 Stat. 1024; Pub. L. 85–207, § 18, Aug. 28, 1957, 71 Stat. 484; Pub. L. 94–521, § 14, Oct. 17, 1976, 90 Stat. 2465.)
Historical and Revision Notes

Based on title 13, U.S.C., 1952 ed., §§ 74, 84, 122, 210, and section 1442 of title 42, U.S.C., 1952 ed., The Public Health and Welfare (Aug. 7, 1916, ch. 274, § 4, 39 Stat. 437; Apr. 2, 1924, ch. 80, § 4, 43 Stat. 32; June 18, 1929, ch. 28, §§ 10, 21, 46 Stat. 24, 26; June 14, 1938, ch. 358, 52 Stat. 678; July 25, 1947, ch. 331, 61 Stat. 457; June 19, 1948, ch. 502, § 2, 62 Stat. 479; July 15, 1949, ch. 338, title VI, § 607, 63 Stat. 441).

Section consolidates parts of sections 74 and 84 of title 13, U.S.C., 1952 ed., relating to cotton statistics and statistics on oilseeds, nuts and kernels, fats, oils and greases (subchapters I and II of chapter 3 of this revised title), all of section 210 of such title, which section was a part of chapter 4 thereof relating to the decennial censuses of population, agriculture, etc. (subchapter II of chapter 5, of this revised title), with that part of section 122 of such title which made such section 210 applicable to the quinquennial censuses of manufactures, the mineral industries, and other businesses provided for in section 121(a) of such title (subchapter I of chapter 5 of this revised title), and, with certain qualifications and exceptions, applicable to the interim surveys provided for by section 121(b) of such title (subchapter IV of chapter 5 of this revised title), and that part of subsection (b) of section 1442 of title 42, U.S.C., 1952 ed., which made such section 210 applicable to the decennial censuses of housing (subchapter II of chapter 5 of this revised title). For remainder of sections 74, 84 and 122 of title 13, U.S.C., 1952 ed., and of section 1442 of title 42, U.S.C., 1952 ed. (which section has been transferred in its entirety to this revised title), see Distribution Table.

Section 210 of title 13, U.S.C., 1952 ed., by its own terms was applicable to the collection of miscellaneous statistics provided for by section 111 of such title (subchapter III of chapter 3 of this revised title), except that such section 111 placed certain restrictions upon the collection of statistics on religion. These restrictions, along with those of section 122 of such title with respect to the making of surveys, and along with provisions excepting this section from application to the censuses of governments provided for by section 251 of title 13, U.S.C., 1952 ed. (subchapter III of chapter 5 of this revised title), are set out as another section in this revised title. Subject to those exceptions and restrictions, this section applies to all collections and censuses provided for in this title, in so far as it is relevant.

Sections 74, 84 and 210 of title 13, U.S.C., 1952 ed., described the same type of offenses, but the penal provisions varied. Section 74 prescribed maximum fine of $1,000 and maximum imprisonment of one year, for refusal to answer or giving a false answer; section 84 prescribed maximum fine of $1,000 for refusal to answer or giving false answer, with no imprisonment; and section 210 prescribed maximum fine of $500 and maximum imprisonment of sixty days for refusal to answer, and maximum fine of $10,000 and maximum imprisonment of one year for giving a false answer. In addition, such section 74 prescribed a minimum fine of $300 for refusal to answer or giving a false answer. This revised section adopts the penalties of such section 210, which was the latest enactment on the subject, and which might have been regarded as having superseded the penal provisions of such sections 74 and 84. According to its own terms, its penal provisions were applicable not only to the censuses of population, agriculture, etc., provided for in chapter 4 of title 13, U.S.C., 1952 ed., but also to any schedules prepared under the act of March 6, 1902 (sections 1–6, 77, 101, 111, and 112 of such title), or under acts amendatory thereof “or supplemental thereto.” This reference did not cover sections 74 and 84 specifically, but such sections, enacted in 1924 and 1916, respectively, could probably be regarded as having been “supplemental” to the 1902 act. In any event, this revised section establishes uniform penalties for refusal to answer, or giving a false answer in the circumstances stated. Further, the prescribed penalties are the maximum, and any lesser penalty can be imposed if the facts of the case warrant it.

Reference to the “Secretary [of Commerce] or other authorized officer or employee of the Department of Commerce or bureau or agency thereof” was substituted for references to the Director of the Census and employees of the Bureau of the Census, to conform with 1950 Reorganization Plan No. 5, §§ 1, 2, eff. May 24, 1950, 15 F.R. 3174, 64 Stat. 1263. See Revision Note to section 4 of this title.

References to the offenses as being in each case a “misdemeanor” were omitted as covered by section 1 of title 18, U.S.C., 1952 ed., Crimes and Criminal Procedure, classifying crimes; and words “upon conviction thereof” and “at the discretion of the court” were omitted as surplusage.

The provision permitting the requests to be made by registered mail, by telegraph, by visiting representative, or by one or more of these methods, was contained in sections 74 and 84 of title 13, U.S.C., 1952 ed., but not in section 210 of such title. It is retained in this section as probably a desirable provision to apply generally.

Provisions in sections 74, 84 and 210 of title 13, U.S.C., 1952 ed., that it “shall be the duty” of the persons referred to, to answer correctly, etc., were omitted as unnecessary and redundant. This section defines offenses and prescribes penalties for committing them, and are deemed sufficient for the purpose of enforcement. However, some of the language used in the omitted provisions was necessarily included in the description of the offenses.

Changes were made in phraseology.

Editorial Notes
Amendments

1976—Pub. L. 94–521 struck out provision enumerating methods by which the Department of Commerce may transmit a request to answer census questions under this section, substituted “schedule or questionnaire” for “schedule”, struck out provision authorizing a sixty day maximum prison term for neglecting or refusing to answer census questions submitted under this section and a similar provision authorizing a one year maximum prison term for willfully giving a false answer to any such questions.

1957—Pub. L. 85–207 inserted “by certified mail,” after “by registered mail,”.

Statutory Notes and Related Subsidiaries
Effective Date of 1976 Amendment

Amendment by Pub. L. 94–521 effective Oct. 17, 1976, see section 17 of Pub. L. 94–521, set out as a note under section 1 of this title.

13 U.S. Code § 225 - Applicability of penal provisions in certain cases

  • U.S. Code
  • Notes
prev | next
(a) In connection with any survey conducted by the Secretary or other authorized officer or employee of the Department of Commerce or bureau or agency thereof pursuant to subchapter IV of chapter 5 of this title, the provisions of sections 221, 222, 223 and 224 of this title shall apply—
(1)
with respect to the answering of questions and furnishing of information, only to such inquiries as are within the scope of the schedules and questionnaires and of the type and character heretofore used in connection with the taking of complete censuses under subchapters I and II of chapter 5 of this title, or in connection with any censuses hereafter taken pursuant to such subchapters;
(2)
only after publication of a determination with reasons therefor certified by the Secretary, or by some other authorized officer or employee of the Department of Commerce or bureau or agency thereof with the approval of the Secretary, that the information called for is needed to aid or permit the efficient performance of essential governmental functions or services, or has significant application to the needs of the public, business, or industry and is not publicly available from nongovernmental or other governmental sources;
(3)
in the case of any new survey, only after public notice, given by the Secretary or other authorized officer or employee of the Department of Commerce or bureau or agency thereof at least thirty days in advance of requesting a return, that such survey is under consideration.
(b)
The provisions for imprisonment provided by section 222 of this title shall not apply in connection with any survey conducted pursuant to subchapter II of chapter 3 of this title, or to subchapter IV of chapter 5 of this title.
(c)
The provisions of sections 221, 222, 223, and 224 of this title shall not apply to any censuses or surveys of governments provided for by subchapters III and IV of chapter 5 of this title, nor to other surveys provided for by subchapter IV of such chapter which are taken more frequently than annually.
(d)
Where the doctrine, teaching, or discipline of any religious denomination or church prohibits the disclosure of information relative to membership, a refusal, in such circumstances, to furnish such information shall not be an offense under this chapter.
(Aug. 31, 1954, ch. 1158, 68 Stat. 1024; Pub. L. 94–521, § 15(a), Oct. 17, 1976, 90 Stat. 2465.)
Historical and Revision Notes

Based on title 13, U.S.C., 1952 ed., §§ 111, 122 (Mar. 2, 1902, ch. 139, § 7, 32 Stat. 52; June 7, 1906, ch. 3048, 34 Stat. 218; June 18, 1929, ch. 28, § 3, 46 Stat. 26; 1939 Reorg. Plan No. II, § 4(e), eff. July 1, 1939, 4 F.R. 2731, 53 Stat. 1431; 1940 Reorg. Plan No. III, § 3, eff. June 30, 1940, 5 F.R. 2107, 54 Stat. 1232; June 25, 1947, ch. 124, 61 Stat. 163; June 19, 1948, ch. 502, § 1, 62 Stat. 478; Sept. 7, 1950, ch. 910, § 4, 64 Stat. 785).

Section consolidates parts of sections 111 and 122 of title 13, U.S.C., 1952 ed., with changes in phraseology necessary to effect consolidation and to preserve the intent, scope and meaning of the parts of such sections so consolidated. For remainder of such sections 111 and 122, see Distribution Table.

Subsections (a) and (b) of this revised section are from section 122 of title 13, U.S.C., 1952 ed., and in subsection (a) references to the Secretary (of Commerce) and to “other authorized officer or employee of the Department of Commerce or bureau or agency thereof” were substituted for references to the Director of the Census to conform with 1950 Reorganization Plan No. 5, §§ 1, 2, eff. May 24, 1950, 15 F.R. 3174, 64 Stat. 1263. See Revision Note to section 4 of this title.

Subsection (c) is partly new (but preserves existing law), and partly from section 122 of title 13, U.S.C., 1952 ed. Section 252 of title 13, U.S.C., 1952 ed., which related to the censuses of governments provided by section 251 thereof (see subchapter III of chapter 5 of this title), made certain sections in chapter 4 of that title relating to censuses of population, agriculture, etc., applicable to such censuses of governments. However, it did not list sections 209 and 210 of such title among the sections made so applicable, probably because they would hardly be relevant and capable of application to such censuses. Subsection (c) makes it clear that sections 221–224 of this revised title, into which were carried the provisions of such sections 209 and 210, and which speak in general terms, are not applicable to the censuses and surveys of governments.

Subsection (d) is from section 111 of title 13, U.S.C., 1952 ed. Words in this subsection, “a refusal, in such circumstances, to furnish such information shall not be an offense under this chapter”, read “such information shall not be required”. It was felt that such exception in such section 111 was actually more in the nature of an exception to the penal provisions, and it has been so treated in this revised title. The collection of statistics on religion are provided for in section 102 of this title.

Editorial Notes
Amendments

1976—Subsec. (a)(1). Pub. L. 94–521, § 15(a)(1), inserted “and questionnaires” after “schedules”.

Subsec. (b). Pub. L. 94–521, § 15(a)(2), struck out reference to imprisonment provisions provided by sections 221 and 224 of this title.

Statutory Notes and Related Subsidiaries
Effective Date of 1976 Amendment

Amendment by Pub. L. 94–521 effective Oct. 17, 1976, see section 17 of Pub. L. 94–521, set out as a note under section 1 of this title.

13 U.S. Code § 191 - Geographic scope of censuses

  • U.S. Code
  • Notes
prev | next
(a)
Each of the censuses authorized by this chapter shall include each State, the District of Columbia, the Virgin Islands, Guam, the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, and the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, and as may be determined by the Secretary, such other possessions and areas over which the United States exercises jurisdiction, control, or sovereignty. Inclusion of other areas over which the United States exercises jurisdiction or control shall be subject to the concurrence of the Secretary of State.
(b)
For censuses taken in the Virgin Islands, Guam, the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, or any possession or area not specifically designated in subsection (a) of this section, the Secretary may use census information collected by the Governor or highest ranking Federal official, if such information was obtained in accordance with plans prescribed or approved by the Secretary.
(c)
If, pursuant to a determination by the Secretary under subsection (a) of this section, any census is not taken in a possession or area over which the United States exercises jurisdiction, control, or sovereignty, the Secretary may include data obtained from other Federal agencies or government sources in the census report. Any data obtained from foreign governments shall be obtained through the Secretary of State.
(Added Pub. L. 85–207, § 14, Aug. 28, 1957, 71 Stat. 483; amended Pub. L. 94–521, § 9, Oct. 17, 1976, 90 Stat. 2463.)

L. 94–521 struck out “(other than censuses of population)” after “this chapter” and “Alaska, Hawaii” after “the District of Columbia”, inserted “the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands” after “Guam”, and struck out provision that censuses of population shall include all geographic areas referred to in first sentence of subsec. (a).

Subsec. (b). Pub. L. 94–521 inserted “the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands” after “Guam”, and substituted “use census information” for “utilize or adopt census data” and “if such information was obtained” for “when such data are obtained”.

Subsec. (c). Pub. L. 94–521 substituted “If, pursuant to a determination by the Secretary under subsection (a) of this section” for “When, under determination by the Secretary as provided in paragraph (a) above”.

Admission of Alaska and Hawaii to Statehood

Alaska was admitted into the Union on Jan. 3, 1959, on issuance of Proc. No. 3269, Jan. 3, 1959, 24 F.R. 81, 73 Stat. c16, and Hawaii was admitted into the Union on Aug. 21, 1959, on issuance of Proc. No. 3309, Aug. 21, 1959, 24 F.R. 6868, 73 Stat. c74. For Alaska Statehood Law, see Pub. L. 85–508, July 7, 1958, 72 Stat. 339, set out as a note preceding section 21 of Title 48, Territories and Insular Possessions. For Hawaii Statehood Law, see Pub. Overview of FY2026 Appropriations for the Census Bureau

September 2, 2025 – March 19, 2026 IF13105

Overview of FY2026 Appropriations for the Census Bureau
Updated March 19, 2026 (IF13105)

Introduction

As a Department of Commerce agency, the U.S. Census Bureau is primarily funded through the annual Commerce, Justice, Science, and Related Agencies (CJS) appropriations bill. This In Focus provides an overview of FY2026 appropriations for the U.S. Census Bureau; certain comparisons to previous years' appropriations; and congressional action to date. Information presented is drawn from the Census Bureau's FY2026 Congressional Budget Justification, the enacted FY2026 CJS bill, and other relevant congressional documents.

The FY2026 appropriations are divided between two accounts: Current Surveys and Programs, and Periodic Censuses and Programs. For these two accounts, comparisons are made here between the FY2026 enacted level, the FY2026 request, and enacted amounts for FY2024 and FY2025. (The FY2025 full-year continuing resolution [CR] funded these accounts in the same amounts and under the same authorities and conditions as enacted in FY2024.) The FY2026 budget justification also includes requested amounts below the account level in more detail, which are compared here to corresponding actual FY2024 amounts (the budget justification document does not provide this level of detail for FY2025 actual amounts).

Figure 1. Census Budget Authority

Source: Data from U.S. Census Bureau, FY2026 Congressional Budget Justification and FY2026 Appropriations.

Notes: Values may not add evenly due to rounding.

FY2026 Appropriations

The enacted FY2026 CJS bill (P.L. 119-74) includes $1.490 billion for the Census Bureau. This is $186 million less than the Trump Administration's FY2026 budget request of $1.677 billion and a $108 million increase from the FY2024 and FY2025 enacted levels of $1.383 billion.

Current Surveys and Programs

The bill includes $319 million for the Current Surveys and Programs account, which is $30 million above the Administration's FY2026 requested $289 million and a decrease of $10 million from the FY2024 and FY2025 enacted amounts of $329 million. This account includes funding for Current Economic Statistics and Current Demographic Statistics.

Current Economic Statistics

Current Economic Statistics include business, construction, manufacturing, general economic, foreign trade, and government statistics. According to the FY2026 budget justification, Current Economic Statistics programs "provide timely, accurate, and essential data on the structure and performance of the U.S. economy, supporting the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) estimation, fiscal and monetary policymaking, and private sector decision-making."

The FY2026 request for Current Economic Statistics was $216 million, the same as FY2024 and FY2025 actual amounts.

Current Demographic Statistics

Current Demographic Statistics includes the Survey of Income and Program Participation (SIPP); the Current Population Survey (CPS), which is sponsored by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) and the Census Bureau; and the Population Estimates Program. The SIPP is an ongoing survey that measures distribution of government assistance programs. The CPS provides estimates of income, poverty, and other indicators. The Population Estimates Program calculates population change over time. The Census Bureau's population estimates are used in a variety of federal programs to determine funding allocations or eligibility.

The FY2026 request for Current Demographic Statistics was $73 million, which is a $40 million decrease from FY2024 and FY2025 actual amounts of $113 million.

Proposed changes to these programs include testing internet self-response for the CPS and using some nonsurvey data to reduce costs for the SIPP.

Periodic Censuses and Programs

The bill includes $1.172 billion for the Periodic Censuses and Programs account, which is $216 million less than the Administration's FY2026 requested $1.388 billion and a $118 million increase from the FY2024 and FY2025 enacted amount of $1.054 billion. This account consists of funding for several programs discussed below.

Decennial Census

The FY2026 request for the decennial census account was $983 million, a $383 million increase from the FY2024 actual amount of $600 million. Requested FY2026 funding for the decennial census includes support for the 2026 Census Test and preparation for the 2028 Dress Rehearsal, full-scale development of core IT infrastructure, award and management of contracts, and continued data collection and publication for the American Community Survey (ACS). Unlike previous budget documents, the FY2026 budget justification does not specify the respective amounts for the 2030 decennial census and the ACS within the decennial census account.

Periodic Economic Statistics

The FY2026 request for the Periodic Economic Statistics Program, which contains the Economic Census and the Census of Governments, was $144 million, an $18 million decrease from the FY2024 actual level of $162 million. Specific funding levels for these two surveys are not provided in the FY2026 budget request.

The Economic Census, conducted every five years, collects statistics on businesses in the United States to help understand the U.S. economy. Requested FY2026 activities for the Economic Census include the continued review of 2022 Economic Census data releases.

The Census of Governments, conducted every five years, collects statistics on state and local governments across the United States. Requested FY2026 activities for the Census of Governments include the expanded use of administrative records and other data collection methods in preparation for the 2027 Census of Governments.

Geographic Support Program

The purpose of the Census Bureau's Geographic Support Program (GSP) is to support and maintain the geospatial infrastructure required to conduct survey data collection, processing, tabulation, and dissemination across covered regions. The Census Bureau considers the GSP to be foundational for all of its social and economic data products. Congressional district wall maps are produced by the GSP. The Census Bureau aims to utilize the GSP to minimize 2030 Census in-field enumeration costs.

The FY2026 request for the GSP was $98 million, a $14 million decrease from the FY2024 and FY2025 actual level of $112 million.

Enterprise Data Collection and Dissemination Systems (EDCaDS)

The EDCaDS generally supports the data collection, processing, and dissemination systems that are associated with Census Bureau programs.

The FY2026 request's stated goal for the EDCaDS is "to provide large cyclical systems that must be scaled for peak operations for the Decennial Census, the Economic Census, and the Census of Governments."

The FY2026 request for the EDCaDS was $163 million, a $17 million decrease from the FY2024 and FY2025 actual level of $180 million.

Congressional Action

The House Appropriations Committee CJS subcommittee marked up the House version of the FY2026 CJS appropriations bill on July 15, 2025. The bill, as approved by the subcommittee, would have provided $1.677 billion in total for the Census Bureau: $288.5 million for Current Surveys and Programs and $1.388 billion for Periodic Censuses and Programs. The bill, as reported, would have prohibited the Census Bureau from using any funds provided in the measure to include "aliens who are unlawfully present in the United States" in rendering apportionment determinations. It also included similar prohibitions on using any funds provided to enforce mandatory response requirements for certain Census Bureau surveys or to inquire more than twice to solicit voluntary survey responses. These provisions were not included in the version of the bill subsequently enacted into law. The bill advanced from the subcommittee by a 9-6 vote. The full committee ordered the bill reported by a 34-28 vote on September 10, 2025.

The Senate Appropriations Committee marked up its FY2026 CJS appropriations bill on July 17, 2025. The bill, as reported, would have provided $1.520 billion in total for the Census Bureau: $328.5 million for Current Surveys and Programs and $1.192 billion for Periodic Census and Programs. Furthermore, the committee report accompanying the bill directs the Census Bureau to provide information regarding the removal of Census and BEA data sets; the termination of Census Bureau advisory committees; ACS modernization efforts; 2030 decennial census operation plans; and the effects of field office closures. The report directs the Census Bureau to continue outreach to public libraries as partners for surveys and to prioritize carrying out the 2026 Census Test. The committee ordered the bill reported by a 19-10 vote.

Census Bureau appropriations lapsed from October 1 through November 12, 2025. The lapse ended when a CR providing appropriations for certain agencies (including the Commerce Department) through January 30, 2026, became law. The FY2026 CJS appropriations bill was included as part of a consolidated appropriations measure, which passed the House by a vote of 397-28 on January 8, 2026, and passed the Senate by a vote of 82-15 on January 15, 2026. The bill was signed into law by President Trump on January 23, 2026. The explanatory statement for the FY2026 CJS bill was filed in the Congressional Record by the chair of the House Appropriations Committee on January 8, 2026. The explanatory statement specifies that the Appropriations Committee reports accompanying the House and Senate versions of the FY2026 CJS appropriations bill carry "the same weight as language included in this joint explanatory statement and should be complied with unless specifically addressed to the contrary in this joint explanatory statement or in the act."

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Economic Census
Description: The Economic Census is the official five-year measure of businesses in the United States providing comprehensive statistics at the national, state, and local levels. It serves as the benchmark for current economic activity, such as the Gross Domestic Product and Producer Price Index.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Economic Census: Research and Preservation Report

**Publisher:** U.S. Census Bureau, U.S. Department of Commerce  
**Frequency:** Every five years, covering reference years ending in **2** and **7**  
**Latest reference year identified in the official releases reviewed:** **2022**  
**Research checked:** October 9, 2026  
**Scope of this report:** The Economic Census program as a whole, with particular attention to the 2022 edition. Historical editions have different coverage, classifications, and dissemination arrangements.

## Executive findings

**Your title and description are accurate.** The Census Bureau’s [Economic Census homepage](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/economic-census.html) uses essentially the same description you supplied, including its role as a benchmark for gross domestic product and the Producer Price Index.

However, four qualifications are essential:

1. **The Economic Census is a collection of statistical products, not one downloadable dataset.** It includes geographic summaries, industry statistics, product statistics, business-size distributions, concentration statistics, classification bridges, and separate island-area products.
2. **“Comprehensive” does not mean all economic activity.** Its core universe is employer establishments in covered industries. Nonemployer businesses, most government establishments, and several industries are excluded.
3. **“Census” does not mean every establishment completes a questionnaire.** Published statistics combine direct responses, administrative records, imputation, and—for certain detailed statistics—sample-based estimates.
4. **It benchmarks GDP and PPI; it does not itself publish those indicators.** The Bureau of Economic Analysis produces GDP, while the Bureau of Labor Statistics produces PPI.

**Preservation assessment:** This is a high-priority federal statistical resource. Its significance extends beyond its own tables because it supports other economic statistics, business decisions, policy analysis, and historical research. A useful preservation effort must capture **data, metadata, classifications, questionnaires, quality information, and release versions together**.

## 1. Identity, publisher, and institutional responsibility

The **U.S. Census Bureau**, within the **Department of Commerce**, conducts and publishes the Economic Census. Businesses and other covered organizations provide responses; the Bureau supplements those responses with administrative information and produces disclosure-protected statistics.

The most useful distinction is between:

| Level | What it represents |
|---|---|
| **Program** | The recurring Economic Census |
| **Edition/reference year** | For example, the 2022 Economic Census |
| **Product family** | Geographic Area Statistics, Product Statistics, Establishment and Firm Size Statistics, etc. |
| **Table or API dataset** | A specific published statistical resource |
| **Release version** | Original, revised, or subsequently corrected data |

For example, the 2022 summary API dataset is **`2022/ecnbasic`**, while the principal all-sector table is **`EC2200BASIC`**. These identifiers are related but are not interchangeable.

**Cataloging implication:** A library should maintain a parent record for the program and more specific records for editions and products. “Economic Census” alone is not sufficiently precise to identify the data underlying an analysis.

Sources: [2022 program overview](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/economic-census/year/2022/about.html); [2022 summary API description](https://api.census.gov/data/2022/ecnbasic.html).

## 2. Legal authority, mandate, and confidentiality

### A. Collection and publication are statutory duties

The principal mandate is **13 U.S.C. §131**, titled *Collection and publication; five-year periods*. It directs the Secretary of Commerce to **take, compile, and publish** censuses of manufactures, mineral industries, and other businesses, including distributive trades, service establishments, and covered transportation activity.

The statute specifies collection years and requires each census to concern the preceding year. Thus, the **2022 reference-year census was collected beginning in 2023**. Reference years ending in 2 and 7 should not be confused with collection or publication years.

Source: [Official U.S. Code, §131](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=%28title%3A13+section%3A131+edition%3Aprelim%29).

### B. Participation is mandatory for organizations selected to report

The Census Bureau’s 2022 respondent information cites **Title 13, §§131, 182, 191, 224, and 225** as authority for the collection and reporting requirement.

- **§224** addresses failure to answer business-related census questions and willfully false answers.
- **§225** governs the applicability of penal provisions in certain circumstances.
- **§191** establishes geographic scope, including specified territories and other areas as determined under the statute.

This is not a voluntary opinion survey. However, mandatory participation does **not** mean every business receives a questionnaire.

Sources: [2022 respondent information](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/economic-census/year/2022/information.html); [§224](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/13/224); [§225](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/13/225); [§191](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/13/191).

### C. Confidentiality is fundamental to the program

Under **13 U.S.C. §9**, information supplied under Title 13 is protected against identifiable publication and nonstatistical use, subject to the statute’s specified exceptions. Individual reports may be examined only by authorized sworn personnel.

The law also protects census-report copies retained by respondents: those copies are immune from legal process and generally cannot be used in proceedings without the respondent’s consent.

**Public-access implication:** The openly available resource is primarily **aggregate statistical data**, not a directory containing named businesses and their confidential financial reports. A preservation project should archive public releases—not seek or redistribute confidential source records.

Sources: [§9](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/13/9); [2022 overview: legal authority and confidentiality](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/economic-census/year/2022/about.html).

### D. Other oversight and funding considerations

The statutory mandate should be distinguished from:

- Congressional appropriations that fund implementation;
- Office of Management and Budget information-collection review under the Paperwork Reduction Act;
- Statistical quality and disclosure-review procedures.

For an institutional archive, the edition-specific OMB clearance, supporting statements, burden estimates, and Federal Register notices are valuable companion records.

**Research limitation:** This report does not establish a complete set of OMB control numbers, an edition-specific total cost, or the applicable federal records-retention schedules. Those require separate administrative-document research; figures should not be inferred from the dataset’s public description.

## 3. Historical development

The Economic Census has roots in nineteenth-century manufacturing enumeration, but it is **not a consistently defined time series extending unchanged to 1810**.

| Period | Development and significance |
|---|---|
| **1810** | First census of manufactures, conducted alongside population enumeration. |
| **1902** | Congress established a permanent Census Bureau and directed five-year manufacturing censuses. |
| **1905** | Manufacturing census conducted separately from the decennial population census. |
| **1930** | First census of business covering retail and wholesale trade; its statistics concerned 1929 activity. Service coverage expanded afterward. |
| **World War II** | Periodic economic censuses were suspended in favor of wartime statistical work. |
| **1947–1948** | Manufacturing and business censuses resumed. |
| **1953–1954** | Funding constraints threatened continuation. The Watkins Commission’s review supported resumption. |
| **1954 reference year** | First fully integrated economic census, using consistent periods, concepts, classifications, and reporting units across sectors; UNIVAC I was used for processing. |
| **1963 onward** | Administrative records supplied basic statistics for very small firms, reducing reporting burden. |
| **1967 reference year onward** | Modern reference-year pattern of years ending in 2 and 7; construction coverage became regular. |
| **1992** | Major expansion into additional transportation industries, finance, insurance, real estate, communications, and utilities. |
| **1997** | First major Economic Census release using NAICS instead of SIC; all published data became accessible on the Internet. |
| **2007** | Printed reports and publication on physical discs were discontinued. |
| **2022** | Agricultural support activities were added to the states/DC program; electronic collection included improved activity-search and adaptive questionnaire functionality. |

The current statutory schedule was established through the **1964 amendment to §131**, leading to the 1967 reference-year census. This is more precise than treating 1967 as necessarily the date of the legislative change.

### Dissemination history matters for preservation

The Bureau documents electronic dissemination beginning with computer tapes in **1972**, CD-ROM publication in **1987**, DVD-ROM publication in **2002**, and discontinuation of discs in **2007**.

A historical archive may therefore need to preserve:

- Printed volumes and scanned page images;
- Legacy machine-readable files and their record layouts;
- CD/DVD contents and any accompanying software;
- Web-era downloads and metadata.

Sources: [Census Bureau history](https://www.census.gov/about/history/historical-censuses-and-surveys/census-programs-surveys/economic-census.html); [historical development working paper](https://www2.census.gov/library/working-papers/2010/econ/economic-census-historical-development.pdf); [§131 amendment history](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=%28title%3A13+section%3A131+edition%3Aprelim%29); [2022 methodology](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/economic-census/year/2022/technical-documentation/methodology.html).

## 4. What the data cover—and what they omit

### A. Statistical units

The basic unit is generally the **establishment**: a single physical location where business, services, or industrial operations occur.

A **firm or company** consists of one or more establishments under common ownership or control. Some industries use alternative reporting arrangements, such as consolidated reporting for multiple establishments.

**Do not equate establishments with firms.** A chain with 100 stores may contribute many establishments but only one firm. Firm counts also require care when aggregating across industries or geographic areas.

### B. Core 2022 universe

For the states/DC program, the target population consists of establishments that:

- Operated for at least part of 2022;
- Were located in the 50 states, District of Columbia, or associated offshore areas;
- Had paid employees;
- Belonged to an in-scope industry;
- Were generally not government-owned, except for specified industries.

Covered sectors include mining, utilities, construction, manufacturing, wholesale and retail trade, transportation and warehousing, information, finance and insurance, real estate, professional services, management, administrative services, selected education, health care, arts and recreation, accommodation and food services, other services, and limited agricultural support activities.

The Bureau describes the 2022 edition as covering **19 sectors and more than 950 detailed industries**.

### C. Important exclusions

For the 2022 states/DC program, excluded categories include:

| Category | Exclusions or qualifications |
|---|---|
| **Nonemployer businesses** | Businesses without paid employees are outside the core employer census. |
| **Agriculture and natural-resource activities** | Crop production, animal production/aquaculture, forestry/logging, fishing/hunting/trapping, and forestry support are excluded. **NAICS 1151 and 1152**, crop and animal-production support, are included. |
| **Transportation** | Rail transportation and Postal Service. |
| **Finance** | Funds, trusts, and other financial vehicles. |
| **Education** | Elementary/secondary schools, junior colleges, colleges, universities, and professional schools. |
| **Organizations** | Religious organizations, labor unions and similar organizations, political organizations. |
| **Households and government** | Private households and public administration. |
| **Government-owned establishments** | Generally excluded, with exceptions including hospitals, certain liquor-related activities, publishers, central banking, and specified gambling activities. |

Covered private nonprofit organizations are not automatically excluded merely because they are tax-exempt.

**Policy implication:** An “all sectors” Economic Census total means **all covered sectors**, not the entire economy. For instance, it does not fully represent public utilities, public libraries, public transit, or the nonemployer economy.

Sources: [2022 methodology](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/economic-census/year/2022/technical-documentation/methodology.html); [industry coverage guidance](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/economic-census/year/2022/guidance/understanding-naics.html).

### D. Island areas are separate products

The program also publishes data for:

- Puerto Rico;
- U.S. Virgin Islands;
- Guam;
- American Samoa;
- Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands.

These products have **separate methodology and coverage documentation**. They should not be assumed to be included in the states/DC national totals or to share every feature of the main program.

Source: [2022 Island Areas methodology](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/economic-census/island-areas/methodology/2022-methodology.html).

## 5. Variables, classifications, and geographic detail

### A. Common measures

The principal statistics include:

- Number of establishments;
- Number of firms, where published;
- Employment;
- Annual payroll;
- Sales, value of shipments, or revenue;
- Primary business activity/industry;
- Product and service revenue;
- Sector-specific measures.

Selected industries also report inventories, operating expenses, materials and fuels, capital expenditures, worker hours, construction activity, benefits costs, or other specialized items.

Examples from the 2022 basic API:

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ESTAB` | Number of establishments |
| `FIRM` | Number of firms |
| `EMP` | Number of employees |
| `PAYANN` | Annual payroll, **$1,000** |
| `RCPTOT` | Sales, value of shipments, or revenue, **$1,000** |
| `NAICS2022` | 2022 NAICS industry code |
| `TAXSTAT` | Tax-status category |
| `TYPOP` | Type-of-operation category |
| `_F` fields | Flags and annotations |
| `_IMP` fields | Imputation-percentage ranges for specified measures |

**Units warning:** Monetary columns frequently use thousands of dollars. Employment has its own reference-period definition; it should not automatically be interpreted as annual-average employment, unique workers, or full-time equivalents.

Sources: [API variable metadata](https://api.census.gov/data/2022/ecnbasic/variables.json); [all-sector table metadata](https://api.census.gov/data/2022/ecnbasic/groups/EC2200BASIC.json); [2022 technical documentation](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/economic-census/year/2022/technical-documentation.html).

### B. Industry and product classifications

- **NAICS—North American Industry Classification System** classifies establishments by business activity.
- **NAPCS—North American Product Classification System** classifies products and services.

Most 2022 industry statistics use **2022 NAICS**, with selected comparative products on a **2017 NAICS basis**. Tables may include 2–6-digit NAICS and selected 7–8-digit NAICS-based detail.

An establishment’s industry and the products it sells are different concepts. A product may be supplied by businesses in multiple industries.

### C. Geographic detail varies substantially

Depending on sector and product, statistics may be published for:

- United States;
- States and DC;
- Counties and equivalents;
- Metropolitan and micropolitan areas;
- Metropolitan divisions;
- Combined statistical areas;
- Economic places and consolidated cities;
- Regions or offshore areas in selected products.

The phrase “national, state, and local” is accurate **for the program overall**, but not a promise that every sector has every geographic level.

Examples:

- Agricultural support, mining, and management-of-companies summary coverage is principally national/state;
- Construction includes national/state/regional coverage;
- Manufacturing includes county and metro coverage but not the same place coverage as many service sectors.

**ZIP-code change:** The Bureau no longer releases Economic Census ZIP-code tables. The most recent are from **2012**. Current ZIP-level employer-business statistics are available through **County/ZIP Code Business Patterns**, but they are not an equivalent replacement for all Economic Census measures.

Sources: [2022 geographic coverage matrix](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/economic-census/geographies/coverage/2022-coverage.html); [API geography metadata](https://api.census.gov/data/2022/ecnbasic/geography.json); [release schedule and ZIP-code notice](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/economic-census/year/2022/news-updates/releases.html).

## 6. How the statistics are produced

### A. Business Register and administrative sources

The Census Bureau selects establishments from its **Business Register**. Register information comes from earlier censuses and surveys and administrative records, notably from the **IRS** and **Social Security Administration**. BLS industry-classification information also supplements the register.

These are protected administrative-data arrangements—not public releases of tax records.

### B. Direct reporting and sampling

The 2022 sample design includes:

1. Active establishments of multi-establishment firms;
2. Large single-establishment firms selected with certainty using industry-specific payroll thresholds;
3. Other establishments selected with certainty for particular reasons;
4. A stratified sample of remaining smaller single-establishment firms.

Other small establishments contribute basic statistics through administrative records or imputation without completing the questionnaire.

The Bureau’s advance 2022 materials described a universe of **over eight million employer establishments**, with approximately **four million** covered through direct collection and administrative records used for the remainder. These are planning-scale figures, not a verified final response count.

### C. Collection and processing

Reporting uses a secure online system. Multi-location companies can use spreadsheet download/upload functionality.

Processing includes:

- Industry classification;
- Logical and consistency edits;
- Comparisons with prior information and administrative sources;
- Follow-up and analyst review;
- Imputation for missing or inconsistent values;
- Allocation of consolidated reports where required;
- Weighting and expansion for sample-based detailed statistics.

For 2022, activity-search functionality used machine learning to suggest classification options from respondents’ descriptions. This is a collection aid, not evidence that published business statistics are simply machine-generated estimates.

### D. Two different estimation situations

**Basic statistics** generally sum information for all known in-scope establishments, using reported, administrative, or imputed values.

**Some industry-specific and product statistics** use weighted sample estimates, with adjustment procedures to align them to relevant totals.

Sources: [2022 methodology](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/economic-census/year/2022/technical-documentation/methodology.html); [2022 talking points](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/economic-census/2022/2022-economic-census-talking-points.pdf).

## 7. Quality, uncertainty, and disclosure protection

### A. No sampling error does not mean no error

The Bureau states that basic measures compiled from all known establishments are **not subject to sampling error**. They remain subject to:

- Coverage error;
- Nonresponse and imputation error;
- Reporting and interpretation errors;
- Classification errors;
- Processing errors;
- Geographic assignment problems.

For sample-based statistics, use published **coefficients of variation, standard errors, or other available uncertainty measures**. These quantify sampling variability, not every source of error.

### B. Response metrics must not be conflated

The 2022 methodology reports:

- A **check-in rate over 73%**;
- A **Unit Response Rate just over 60%**.

These use different definitions. A returned questionnaire is not necessarily sufficient to meet the standard unit-response definition.

Other documented metrics include total quantity response, quantity response, administrative-data, and imputation rates. Selected table fields report imputation ranges—for example, code 0 indicates less than 10%, while code 9 indicates 90% or more.

### C. Suppression and missing rows

For the main program, confidentiality protection includes:

- Primary cell suppression;
- Complementary suppression to prevent deduction from other totals;
- Suppression symbols, commonly **`D`**;
- Nonpublication of rows with fewer than three contributing firms or establishments.

Consequently:

> **A missing row or suppressed value is not evidence of zero economic activity.**

Suppressed values generally remain represented in higher-level totals. Summing visible detail may therefore fail to reproduce a published total.

### D. Island-area noise infusion

Island-area products use **noise infusion** as their primary disclosure-avoidance method. Quantitative records are perturbed before tabulation.

Their published noise flags indicate:

- **G:** less than 2% change;
- **H:** at least 2% but less than 8%;
- **J:** 8% or more.

Do not assume those thresholds or that method apply universally to every Economic Census product. Read the methodology for the specific release.

Sources: [2022 methodology and response metrics](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/economic-census/year/2022/technical-documentation/methodology.html); [data dictionary](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/economic-census/year/2022/technical-documentation/data-dictionary.html); [Island Areas methodology](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/economic-census/island-areas/methodology/2022-methodology.html).

## 9. Typical users and benefits to the public

### A. Federal economic-statistics agencies

**Bureau of Economic Analysis**

The Economic Census supplies primary source information for benchmark **input-output accounts**, which in turn support national income and product accounts and GDP estimates.

For example, BEA’s 2023 comprehensive update benchmarked accounts to the **2017 Economic Census**. This demonstrates both the dependency and the lag between a census reference year and downstream incorporation.

Sources: [BEA input-output accounts](https://www.bea.gov/data/industries/input-output-accounts-data); [2023 comprehensive update](https://apps.bea.gov/scb/issues/2023/11-november/1123-nea-comprehensive-update.htm).

**Bureau of Labor Statistics**

PPI uses Economic Census shipments and revenue data to weight product-line indexes into larger aggregates.

A 2026 BLS notice states that PPI shipment-value weights continued to be based on **2017 Economic Census** values, while certain allocation relationships were updated to the 2017 BEA input-output accounts.

**Important distinction:** The Economic Census supplies weights and structural benchmarks; it is not the monthly collection of prices.

Sources: [BLS PPI weighting FAQ](https://www.bls.gov/ppi/faqs/questions-and-answers.htm); [2026 allocation update](https://www.bls.gov/ppi/notices/2026/ppi-updates-to-2017-commodity-weight-allocations-for-the-final-demand-intermediate-demand-aggregation-structure.htm).

### B. Businesses and financial institutions

Typical uses include:

- Market sizing and location selection;
- Comparing industry sales, payroll, and employment;
- Identifying supplier or partnership opportunities;
- Preparing business plans and loan applications;
- Evaluating product/service mixes;
- Assessing expansion opportunities.

Its public availability reduces information barriers for small businesses that cannot buy extensive commercial market research.

### C. State and local governments

Uses include:

- Economic-development planning;
- Industry and workforce analysis;
- Tax-policy assessment;
- Grant applications;
- Infrastructure and service planning;
- Emergency preparedness.

### D. Researchers, journalists, trade associations, and advocates

The data support analysis of:

- Industrial restructuring;
- Regional specialization;
- Business size and organization;
- Market concentration;
- Sectoral employment and payroll;
- Geographic disparities in commercial services;
- Long-run economic change.

### E. Documented examples—and a source caveat

The Bureau’s uses page describes examples involving restaurant drive-through expansion, tobacco-product tax policy, small-business planning, grocery-access grants, and disaster preparedness.

However, that page deliberately discusses **Census economic programs broadly**. Some examples combine Economic Census tables with the American Community Survey or other business datasets. ZIP-level examples should not be interpreted as evidence that the 2022 Economic Census publishes ZIP tables.

Source: [Purposes and Uses of Economic Census Data](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/economic-census/guidance/data-uses.html).

### Public-benefit summary

The central public benefits are:

1. A common, publicly accessible evidence base;
2. Better benchmarks for major economic indicators;
3. Comparable industry and geographic statistics;
4. Lower information costs for businesses and communities;
5. More transparent policy debate;
6. A historical record of economic structure.

These are benefits of statistical infrastructure—not proof that any particular policy using the data will succeed.

## 10. Analytical pitfalls and recommended practices

### Essential cautions

| Pitfall | Better practice |
|---|---|
| Treating receipts as GDP | Receipts can include intermediate transactions; GDP measures value added. |
| Comparing identical NAICS codes across years without checking definitions | Use classification concordances, bridge tables, and comparative products. |
| Interpreting nominal growth as real growth | Apply suitable deflators and document the choice. |
| Treating establishments as firms | Select the correct statistical unit. |
| Adding sector and detailed-industry rows together | Keep mutually exclusive aggregation levels. |
| Adding tax-status totals to their components | Retain and filter all categorical dimensions. |
| Replacing suppression with zero | Preserve missingness and disclosure flags. |
| Treating payroll/employment as a typical worker’s annual wage | Recognize reference-period, hours, turnover, and workforce-composition differences. |
| Reading sales/employee as pure productivity | Account for prices, purchased inputs, sector concepts, and employment timing. |
| Inferring causality from two five-year snapshots | Use additional data and a credible research design. |

### Classification and geography change

The **1997 SIC-to-NAICS transition** is a major historical break. Some old industries can be reconstructed from newer ones; others can only be approximated.

For 2022 versus 2017, use the **Comparative Statistics** on a 2017 NAICS basis and **Bridge Statistics** showing classification changes. These do not automatically resolve every local-area comparability issue.

Geographic boundaries and metro definitions also change. Join on geographic identifiers and vintage—not names alone.

Source: [Comparing Historical Economic Census Data](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/economic-census/year/2017/economic-census-2017/guidance/historical-data.html).

### Recommended data-engineering workflow

1. Define the target universe and statistical unit.
2. Choose the appropriate product family.
3. Read sector definitions and coverage before extraction.
4. Acquire data **with flags and categorical dimensions**.
5. Preserve geography and classification codes as strings.
6. Check record uniqueness using all relevant dimensions.
7. Separate totals from components.
8. Retain an untouched source copy.
9. Version transformations, crosswalks, and inflation adjustments.
10. Report suppression, imputation, sampling uncertainty, and coverage limitations.

**Metadata caution:** A classification code appearing in an API’s general code list is not proof that observations for that industry are published in the Economic Census. Verify scope against the coverage documentation and actual records.

## 12. Preservation and data-librarian recommendations

The following are **recommended archival practices**, not claims about an existing complete Census preservation package.

### A. What to preserve

**Data**

- Complete bulk downloads for each product and edition;
- Original compressed files;
- Extracted machine-readable files;
- API responses used in published research;
- Original and revised releases when obtainable;
- Island-area products separately.

**Interpretive materials**

- Dataset and table descriptions;
- Variable, geography, and group metadata;
- Data dictionaries and flag definitions;
- Questionnaires and instructions;
- Methodology and quality statements;
- Sector-specific definitions;
- NAICS/NAPCS code lists and concordances;
- Geographic definitions and boundary vintages;
- Release schedules, errata, and revision notices.

**Administrative and historical context**

- Statutory authority;
- OMB supporting statements and burden documentation;
- Program histories;
- Historical publication inventories;
- Legacy record layouts and software documentation.

### B. Minimum provenance record

For every acquisition, record:

```text

Reference year
Product family
Dataset/API name and table ID
Release or revision date, if known
Retrieval timestamp
Exact source URL or API query
File name, size, and media type
Cryptographic checksum

```

A suitable citation might be:

### C. Principal preservation risks

1. **Revisions under unchanged URLs:** Live data may overwrite earlier values.
2. **Interface migrations:** Interactive applications are not durable archival objects.
3. **Incomplete exports:** A visible table view may omit parts of the dataset.
4. **Lost flags and footnotes:** Numeric-only copies can become misleading.
5. **Classification drift:** Data without the appropriate codebook lose historical meaning.
6. **Legacy media:** Old tapes, discs, and proprietary layouts may require migration.
7. **Fragmented releases:** Products appear over several years.
8. **Restricted microdata:** A public archive cannot reproduce the confidential processing environment.

### D. Recommended preservation design

Maintain:

- An immutable source layer;
- A normalized, documented analysis layer;
- A separately versioned historical-harmonization layer;
- Multiple copies with regular checksum validation;
- A manifest connecting data to documentation;
- Locally assigned persistent identifiers for archived snapshots.

For web documentation, preserve both readable/rendered content and machine-readable captures where practical. A captured page consisting mainly of navigation or scripts is not a successful preservation copy.

### E. Rights and access

Published federal statistical data are generally reusable; U.S. government works are generally outside U.S. copyright protection under **17 U.S.C. §105**. Nevertheless:

- Do not assign a specific Creative Commons license unless supported by the source;
- Check third-party material separately;
- Preserve attribution and provenance;
- Distinguish your modified data from official releases;
- Do not imply Census Bureau endorsement;
- Do not confuse public-domain publication rights with access to confidential records.

**Unresolved archival question:** This review does not establish the retention or eventual transfer rules for every confidential source file or internal processing artifact. Those are separate records-management matters.

## 13. Issues for policy activists and public-interest researchers

### A. Coverage affects whose economic activity is visible

Employer-focused statistics can underrepresent self-employment, independent contracting, and businesses without payroll. Government-service exclusions can also produce incomplete pictures of access to hospitals, utilities, transit, libraries, or education unless complementary data are used.

### B. Local confidentiality protection reduces detail

Small communities and concentrated industries may have more suppression or unpublished rows. This creates a genuine tension between useful local statistics and the legal duty to protect respondents.

Responsible advocacy should ask for better usable statistics and transparent documentation—not identifiable business disclosures.

### C. Five-year benchmarks are not timely local monitoring

Release lags make the Economic Census unsuitable as the sole source for monitoring a current recession, disaster, or rapid business closure. Pair it with more frequent indicators.

### D. Concentration statistics are not antitrust findings

Published concentration ratios can inform debate, but national industry categories do not necessarily match the relevant product and geographic markets in an antitrust analysis. They are evidence, not a legal conclusion.

### E. Sustained funding protects more than one dataset

Historical interruption during World War II and the early-1950s funding crisis illustrate that continuity cannot be taken for granted. The dependency of GDP benchmarking and PPI weighting on Economic Census data makes preservation and continued production broader public-interest concerns.

### F. Reproducibility is a public benefit

Advocates and journalists should publish exact table IDs, editions, filters, flags, and archived source copies where permitted. This allows others to audit claims rather than rely on an unrepeatable interactive view.

# Economic Census: Dataset Risk Assessment

**Assessment date: October 9, 2026**

## Overall finding

**Existing Economic Census data remain publicly accessible, and I found no evidence that the program has been terminated or that its historical files are being systematically withdrawn.** Its explicit statutory mandate and importance to GDP benchmarking, price-index weighting, and business decision-making provide substantial protection.

The more credible risks are **loss of agency capacity, changes to future collection, reduced detail, and delays**, rather than imminent disappearance of all published data.

Two distinctions affect the ratings:

- **Agency-wide evidence is not necessarily Economic Census-specific.** The staffing rating uses Census Bureau losses because your rubric explicitly permits agency-level evidence.
- **The rubric does not limit historical availability or quality changes to January 2025 onward.** Consequently, the quality rating includes the longstanding discontinuation of Economic Census ZIP-code tables. I distinguish that from newer risks below.

These are evidence-based classifications, **not numerical probabilities**. I did not conduct a complete file-by-file integrity audit or establish that every original release version remains available.

## 1. Historical Data Availability

### Evidence supporting **No Known Issue**
- The Bureau’s [data-by-year page](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/economic-census/data/tables.html) continues to provide:
  - Interactive tables and bulk files for **2012, 2017, and 2022**;
  - Bulk files for **2002 and 2007**;
  - Links to historical publications for earlier editions.
- A direct check of the [2017 multi-sector bulk directory](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/economic-census/data/2017/sector00/) returned a publicly accessible listing containing basic statistics, products, business-size statistics, concentration statistics, and island-area files.
- The Bureau states that **previously released ZIP-code tables will remain accessible**, although new Economic Census ZIP tables are no longer produced. See the [release inventory](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/economic-census/year/2022/news-updates/ecdata-releases.html).

### Evidence relevant to **Moderate or High Risk**
- Dissemination methods have changed: older editions do not all have the same interactive interfaces as recent editions. However, **a change of interface is not evidence that the underlying data have disappeared**.
- Statistical corrections and revisions occur. For example, current [2022 bulk listings](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/economic-census/data/2022/sector00/) show later modification dates for some products. This creates a **version-preservation concern**, but does not establish destructive alteration of historical editions.
- I found no verified example of a previously published Economic Census historical file or historical variable being removed from public access during this review.

### Evidence supporting **Gone**
- None found.

### Selected level: **No Known Issue**

Historical editions remain discoverable and accessible through official channels. The main uncertainty concerns **completeness and availability of superseded versions**, not demonstrated removal of prior cycles.

**Confidence: Moderate.** Availability checks and official inventories are reassuring, but they do not substitute for a complete archival audit.

## 2. Future Data Availability

### Evidence supporting **No Known Issue**
- The 2022 edition continued publishing through **April 2026**. The Bureau’s [2026 release log](https://www.census.gov/data/what-is-data-census-gov/latest-releases.2026.html) records Economic Census releases on **April 30, 2026**, including telemedicine and professional-employer-organization tables.
- The updated [2022 release schedule](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/economic-census/year/2022/news-updates/releases.html) anticipated miscellaneous releases through April 2026.
- The FY2027 budget materials support preparation for the **2027 Economic Census**. The Census Project’s [summary of the congressional justification](https://thecensusproject.org/2026/05/01/summary-of-census-bureau-fy2027-congressional-justification/) reports a request of **$166.9 million and 420 FTE**, including a proposed increase of $33 million and 63 FTE. These are **requested**, not verified enacted, resources.
- A [May 20, 2026 Federal Register notice](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/05/20/2026-10118/agency-information-collection-activities-submission-to-the-office-of-management-and-budget-omb-for) proposes reinstating the Commodity Flow Survey, explicitly described as a component of the 2027 Economic Census. This is evidence of continued planning, not final clearance of the main census.

### Evidence supporting **Moderate Risk**
- Earlier official guidance intended completion of the 2022 releases **by March 2026**. The [Economic Census FAQ](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/economic-census/year/2022/about/faq/faq-general.html) retains that expectation.
- Actual final releases occurred **April 30, 2026**. Thus, at least part of publication extended beyond an earlier intended completion date, although it met the later revised schedule.
- Agency staffing losses and uncertainty around the next cycle’s resources create additional forward-looking concerns.

### Evidence relevant to **High Risk: an important ICR distinction**
- Older respondent materials list **June 30, 2025** as the expiration date for OMB control number **0607-0998**, the 2022 Economic Census.
- However, the official [OMB control-number history](https://www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAOMBHistory?ombControlNumber=0607-0998) records a **“Discontinue” action approved March 31, 2025**.
- That action concerns the **2022 collection clearance**. It is not, by itself, evidence that the recurring Economic Census program was terminated or that a required ongoing collection has operated with an expired clearance for more than a year.
- I did **not** verify an active main 2027 Economic Census clearance. That remains a monitoring gap; it is not sufficient evidence to declare a missed clearance deadline or skipped cycle.

### Evidence supporting **Gone**
- None found. Continued publication and next-cycle preparation contradict program termination.

### Selected level: **Moderate Risk**

The strongest rubric-matching evidence is the extension beyond the earlier **March 2026 intended completion date**. The delay was limited and publication subsequently occurred.

**Confidence: Moderate.** This is a conservative rating based on schedule slippage, not evidence that the 2027 census will be canceled.
